title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) & Eval
summary: What DPO optimizes and what it tends to do to likelihoods along the way, how to choose its reference model, how to read its training metrics without mistaking them for quality, and how to evaluate a preference-tuned model with pairwise win rates from a judge whose biases you have controlled.
objectives: Explain how DPO replaces RLHF's reward-model-plus-reinforcement-learning pipeline with a classification loss on chosen and rejected completions relative to a reference policy, and what beta controls.
Prepare a preference dataset in the formats a DPO trainer accepts, and choose a reference model that matches the distribution the preferences were sampled from.
Interpret DPO training metrics -- implicit rewards, margins, reward accuracy, and log-probabilities -- and recognize when a rising margin is not evidence of a better model.
Design a pairwise win-rate evaluation against a named baseline, with controls for judge position, verbosity, and self-preference bias.
Report a preference-tuning result with its trade-offs and failure checks rather than a single headline win rate.

sections.title: From RLHF's two stages to one classification loss
paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback first fits a reward model to human preference labels, then fine-tunes the language model with reinforcement learning to maximize that reward without drifting too far from the original model. The DPO paper (Rafailov et al.) calls this a complex and often unstable procedure. DPO introduces a new parameterization of the reward model under which the optimal policy can be extracted in closed form, so the same RLHF objective can be solved with a simple classification loss -- no separate reward model to train and no sampling from the model during fine-tuning.

The objective DPO optimizes is the familiar one: reward maximization under a KL-divergence constraint that keeps the policy close to a reference. The paper explains why that constraint matters -- it keeps the model near the distribution on which the reward is accurate, maintains generation diversity, and prevents collapse onto a single high-reward answer. In DPO the reward is implicit: it is beta times the log-ratio of the policy's and the reference model's probabilities for a completion.

Hugging Face TRL writes the loss as the negative log-sigmoid of beta times the difference between the chosen completion's log-ratio and the rejected completion's log-ratio, each measured against the reference model. Its DPOConfig sets beta to 0.1 by default and describes it as controlling deviation from the reference: a higher beta means less deviation. TRL also implements a family of alternative losses selected by loss_type -- among them a robust variant that models label noise through label smoothing, and a length-normalized variant aimed at the length bias of the original sigmoid loss.

sections.title: The reference model has to match the data
paragraphs: Every DPO quantity is measured relative to the reference model, so choosing it is a design decision, not a default. The DPO paper points out that public preference datasets were sampled from a particular supervised fine-tuned model, and initializes the reference to that SFT model whenever it is available. When it is not, the authors initialize the reference by maximizing the likelihood of the preferred completions -- a step they call Preferred-FT -- to reduce the distribution shift between the true reference distribution and the one DPO uses. They did exactly this for their single-turn dialogue experiments, where no standard SFT model existed.

In TRL, leaving ref_model unset makes the trainer use the model's own state before DPO training starts. Two options change the memory and behaviour of that reference: precompute_ref_log_probs computes the reference log-probabilities for the whole training set up front so the reference model need not stay in memory, and sync_ref_model periodically mixes the current policy into the reference (the TR-DPO approach), which TRL notes is not yet compatible with PEFT or with precomputed reference log-probabilities.

Each training example is a prompt with one chosen and one rejected completion to that same prompt, in either a standard or conversational format; for conversational data TRL applies the chat template automatically. Because the loss only sees the difference between the two completions, the pair teaches whatever distinguishes them. If the chosen answers are also systematically longer or more formatted than the rejected ones, that difference is part of what the model learns.
sections.callout: Before training, write down which model generated the preference data and which model is your reference. If they are not the same, you are relying on DPO to bridge a distribution shift.

sections.title: Reading DPO metrics without fooling yourself
paragraphs: TRL logs the quantities DPO is actually moving. rewards/chosen and rewards/rejected are the average implicit rewards -- beta times the policy-to-reference log-ratio -- for the chosen and rejected completions. rewards/margins is the average difference between them, and rewards/accuracies is the proportion of pairs in which the chosen completion's implicit reward exceeds the rejected one's. logps/chosen and logps/rejected report the average log-probabilities the model assigns to each.

TRL's own description of the method explains how those numbers usually move: DPO widens the margin between preferred and dispreferred log-likelihoods relative to the reference, and in practice this is typically achieved by suppressing the likelihood of dispreferred completions rather than by increasing the likelihood of preferred ones. So a climbing margin and a reward accuracy near 1 on training pairs say the model has learned to separate those pairs. They do not say its own generations on new prompts are better, and a growing margin says nothing on its own about whether the chosen answers became more likely -- watch logps/chosen and logps/rejected separately.

Because the implicit reward is measured against the reference, it is also a measure of how far the policy has moved. The DPO paper insists that comparisons account for both reward and divergence from the reference: slightly higher reward at much higher KL is not necessarily desirable. It also lists reward over-optimization in the DPO setting as an open question, asking whether a slight decrease in performance over the course of training in one of its own experiments is an instance of it. Treat training metrics as diagnostics, and decide quality with generations on held-out prompts.

sections.title: Evaluating with pairwise win rates
paragraphs: When a ground-truth reward function exists, the paper evaluates DPO by its frontier of achieved reward against KL-divergence from the reference. For real tasks, where no ground-truth reward is known, it evaluates by win rate against a baseline, using GPT-4 as a proxy for human judgment: for summarization the baseline is the test set's reference summaries, and for dialogue it is the preferred response in the test data. Completions were sampled across temperatures from 0.0 to 1.0, and the paper reports DPO as more robust to sampling temperature than PPO.

The same paper shows why the judge is part of the experiment. Its human study found GPT-4's agreement with humans typically similar to or higher than agreement between human annotators -- but also that GPT-4, asked simply which summary was better, preferred longer and more repetitive summaries than humans did, so the authors added a prompt that also asked for concision, and they note that win rates are affected by the judge prompt. They also re-evaluated their summarization policies on news articles from a different dataset, to see how the policies behaved under a distribution shift.

A usable evaluation plan follows from that: name the baseline explicitly (usually the reference or SFT model you started from), fix and version the judge prompt, sample at more than one temperature, and hold out a prompt set from a different distribution than the training preferences.

sections.title: Controlling the judge
paragraphs: The MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena study (Zheng et al.) catalogues the judge's failure modes: position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias, and limited reasoning ability. In its position-bias test, built from pairs of very similar answers, most LLM judges favoured the answer shown first, and only GPT-4 gave consistent verdicts across swapped orders in more than 60% of cases. Verbosity bias is a preference for longer responses even when they are not clearer or more accurate. After controlling for these, the study found strong judges reached over 80% agreement with human preferences -- the same level as agreement between humans.

The study's conservative fix for position bias is simple: call the judge twice with the answers swapped, declare a win only when the same answer wins in both orders, and count an inconsistent pair as a tie. Randomizing positions is the more aggressive alternative, workable at scale. On self-enhancement bias -- a judge favouring answers generated by itself -- the study could not reach a conclusion from its limited data, while the QLoRA authors observed GPT-4 rating its own outputs markedly higher than human raters did, and also reported strong order effects and only weak sample-level agreement between GPT-4 and human annotators on their chatbot evaluation.

The QLoRA paper adds a caution about benchmarks as a complement to win rates: strong MMLU performance did not imply strong chatbot performance, and results appeared to depend on how similar the fine-tuning data was to each benchmark. For a preference-tuned model, report the swap-consistent win rate, a capability check the tuning should not have damaged, and a small human-labelled slice to calibrate the judge.
sections.callout: If you cannot say how often your judge changes its verdict when the answers swap places, you do not yet know what your win rate means.

sections.title: Practical lab scope and evidence boundaries
paragraphs: This lab trains a real, finite-response conditional categorical policy on a CPU using only the Python standard library. It first performs supervised fine-tuning on chosen completions, freezes that result as the reference, and then minimizes the sigmoid DPO loss with analytic gradients at beta 0.1 and beta 0.5. The policy parameters actually change. This is not a spreadsheet or a simulator of optimization.

The model has a fixed response vocabulary and shared prompt features. It can demonstrate gradient direction, reference-relative rewards, held-out transfer through shared features, sampling, and evaluation controls. It cannot demonstrate transformer language ability, tokenization effects, free-form generation quality, accelerator behavior, or the performance of any real LLM. Its results are not evidence about Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, or any other model family.

The implementation follows the sigmoid DPO objective described by the DPO paper and TRL. For each pair, z equals beta times the policy-minus-reference log-probability difference for the chosen completion minus the corresponding difference for the rejected completion, and the loss is negative log sigmoid of z. See https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290 and https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/dpo_trainer.

No execution of the supplied program is claimed here. Numeric snapshots, hashes, sampled text, and aggregate metrics are computed and printed by the program when the learner runs it. The expected results stated in this lab are algebraic invariants enforced by assertions, not invented run logs.
sections.callout: Treat the tiny run as an executable mechanics check. Full-scale transformer training and human evaluation remain separate acceptance evidence.

sections.title: Run actual SFT, frozen-reference DPO, and evaluation
paragraphs: Save this code as lab.py in the same directory as fixtures.json, then run python lab.py. It requires Python 3.10 or later and no third-party packages. The loader creates defensive immutable tuples from the JSON input. Model construction and both trainers return new dictionaries rather than mutating their arguments.

The SFT gradient is ordinary categorical cross-entropy on each chosen response. DPO then starts from the frozen SFT reference. For a pair, the derivative with respect to the chosen logit is negative beta times sigmoid of negative z, while the rejected derivative has the opposite sign. Gradient descent therefore raises the chosen-minus-rejected logit difference. Each DPO update asserts that a sufficiently small update decreases that pair's loss.

The finite-difference check compares the analytic derivative with a central numerical derivative. It also checks that the optimizer's actual chosen-feature update equals negative learning rate times the numerical gradient within tolerance. This would fail for the rejected implementation's former ascent sign.

Metrics are calculated from one policy per beta. Each record includes chosen and rejected policy log-probabilities, chosen and rejected implicit rewards, reward margin, and reward accuracy. Records cover the frozen reference before DPO and the resulting policy after DPO on train, in-distribution holdout, and shifted holdout data.

Generation uses independent seeded categorical samples at temperatures 0.5 and 1.2. The deterministic rubric judge first checks the prompt-specific required answer and then prefers a shorter string only when correctness is tied. It judges both orders. A win or loss is recorded only if both orders select the same response identity; inconsistent verdicts become ties. Swap consistency is calculated from the two verdicts rather than hardcoded. A deliberately position-biased judge is tested as a negative case.

For verbosity analysis, the report computes character lengths only for decisive winners and losers. If no decisive comparison exists, the relevant mean is null, meaning UNKNOWN. The sampled response strings are included in every evaluation record.
sections.callout: The rubric is transparent and deterministic, but it is not an LLM judge. Its verdicts test evaluation plumbing, not semantic quality.

sections.title: Expected output and how to inspect it
paragraphs: Run python lab.py from the directory containing both files. The exact numeric METRICS values, hashes, parameter snapshots, and sampled strings are UNKNOWN in this written artifact because no execution is claimed. Running the supplied files with a conforming Python 3.10 or later interpreter establishes them. The run is deterministic for the same files and Python mathematical behavior because every sample uses an explicit local seed.

A successful run prints initial, SFT-reference, and two DPO parameter snapshots. It prints before and after metrics for train, in_holdout, and shifted at each beta. Every metrics object contains logps_chosen, logps_rejected, rewards_chosen, rewards_rejected, rewards_margin, and rewards_accuracy. Every evaluation object contains actual policy_text and reference_text samples, win/tie/loss counts, derived swap consistency, and winner-versus-loser character lengths.

The reference-versus-itself before records must have zero chosen reward, zero rejected reward, zero reward margin, and zero reward accuracy because the code uses the strict comparison chosen reward greater than rejected reward. For both beta values, the asserted training reward margin and reward accuracy must increase. Each individual DPO update must lower its current pair loss. These properties follow from applying gradient descent to negative log sigmoid of z with the chosen and rejected gradients in opposite directions.

The exact final line is ALL_CHECKS PASS. Before it, the run must print PASS lines for the finite-difference derivative, the optimizer's negative numerical-gradient direction, duplicate split rejection, equal-pair rejection, empty-completion rejection, nonfinite-beta rejection, reference mutation protection, zero-step invariance, position-bias detection, loss decrease at both beta values, margin improvement at both beta values, and frozen-reference preservation. If any check fails, Python raises an exception instead of printing ALL_CHECKS PASS.

sections.title: Changed-input practice task
paragraphs: Complete this task after the unchanged lab passes. Work on a copy of fixtures.json. In the training record whose prompt is customer reply, change chosen from calm to angry and rejected from angry to calm. Do not alter features, holdouts, judge_expected, random seeds, optimization settings, or any other training pair.

Before running, write predictions for four traceable decisions: the immediate DPO gradient direction for the tone weights of angry and calm; whether the changed row's chosen-minus-rejected margin should rise during its own updates; which untouched in-distribution prompt shares the affected feature; and why the transparent judge can disagree with the new training preference.

Run the modified fixture and preserve its stdout separately. Compare the SFT-reference snapshot, each DPO snapshot, tone-holdout metrics, and sampled polite support note text with the original run. Do not predict that every sample must change. Seeded categorical sampling can return the same text even when probabilities change.

Hints: trace the tone feature from customer reply to polite support note. For any row, gradient descent on the sigmoid DPO loss raises the current chosen logit and lowers the current rejected logit. The policy never reads judge_expected.
sections.callout: Make predictions before reading the key. A changed sample is possible, not guaranteed.

sections.title: Changed-input practice key and feedback
paragraphs: Decision 1: for the edited row, the DPO update increases the tone weight and shared bias contribution for angry and decreases those contributions for calm. This follows directly from chosen plus equals learning rate times beta times sigmoid of negative z, with the rejected update carrying the opposite sign.

Decision 2: the edited row's chosen-minus-rejected reference-relative margin rises during its own sufficiently small updates, and its pair loss falls. The program checks loss decrease after every update. Interactions with the remaining calm-over-angry team message mean the final aggregate tone result depends on both conflicting rows, so do not claim the final calm or angry parameter sign without inspecting the snapshot.

Decision 3: polite support note is the untouched in-distribution prompt that shares the tone feature. Team message is also relevant, but it is a training prompt rather than a holdout. Because weights are shared by feature, the edited row can change held-out probabilities without prompt overlap or a prompt-specific answer lookup.

Decision 4: the judge still requires calm for polite support note because judge_expected was deliberately left unchanged. Training preferences and evaluation rules are separate inputs. A judge loss after the edit is therefore not an optimizer failure. It indicates that the changed preference conflicts with the evaluation rubric.

If you predicted that angry must be the final sample, revise the claim to a probability-direction statement. If you predicted no holdout effect because prompt strings differ, inspect the shared tone feature. If you changed judge_expected to make the policy win, restore it because that would move the evaluation target after seeing the training intervention.
sections.callout: The key establishes gradient and data-flow consequences. It does not claim a particular sampled string or final numeric metric without execution.

sections.title: Transfer contract for a real transformer and human evaluation
paragraphs: The practical lab has two evidence boundaries. The standard-library categorical policy is a runnable offline mechanics exercise. The supplied causal-transformer lab is real PyTorch gradient training, but it is a miniature randomly initialized model trained on synthetic arithmetic. Neither is evidence about pretrained capability or production quality. A full-scale pretrained adapter remains unimplemented and pending.

Clone or download the public learner repository from https://github.com/project42dev/project42-content/tree/main/training/rag-and-fine-tuning-engineering/dpo-and-model-evaluation/lab, then change into training/rag-and-fine-tuning-engineering/dpo-and-model-evaluation/lab before running the commands. The relevant files are dpo_transformer_lab.py, requirements.lock, the offline exercise, fixtures, and the human-label CSV. Do not replace these with private paths or an invented URL. The transformer entrypoint is dpo_transformer_lab.py. Dependency installation and training runtime are environment-dependent and UNKNOWN until measured in the learner's environment.

For a provider-neutral transfer, candidates may include Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, NVIDIA, Z.ai, and Kimi, as well as commercial model families used only as evaluation candidates. These names do not establish availability, suitability, license permission, hosting, architecture compatibility, tokenizer compatibility, or quality. Check the selected provider's architecture, tokenizer, chat template, context rules, license, hosting arrangement, checkpoint format, and adapter support before implementation. The custom transformer cannot directly ingest an external checkpoint.

Preserve the contract: prompt, chosen, and rejected records; completion-only log-probabilities; a chosen-completion SFT reference that remains frozen; independent policy copies; beta 0.1 and 0.5; held-out and shifted prompts; two declared temperatures; saved generations; both judge orders; inconsistent verdicts scored as ties; length diagnostics; and a human-label file whose empty fields remain pending. Record exact model and tokenizer revisions, seed, software, hardware, data provenance, commands, and artifact hashes. The contract is complete only after actual files and stdout are archived and reviewed.

The reference should match the preference-data generator when possible. If that generator is unavailable, the DPO paper's Preferred-FT procedure is a documented alternative. TRL documents prompt/chosen/rejected and conversational formats, reference handling, precomputed reference log-probabilities, and DPO metrics at https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/dpo_trainer. The method is described at https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290. Judge limitations and swap-order controls are discussed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685.
sections.callout: Full-scale acceptance is pending until a pinned environment, complete datasets, actual transformer artifacts, raw swapped-order judgments, and independently completed human labels are available. Do not claim installation, training, quality, or agreement that has not been executed and reviewed.

sections.title: Trace DPO arithmetic before transformer training
paragraphs: Use the supplied offline exercise to make signs and scaling auditable. In the worked case, chosen log-ratio = -1.2 - (-1.4) = 0.2 and rejected log-ratio = -2.0 - (-1.8) = -0.2. At beta 0.1, chosen reward is 0.02, rejected reward is -0.02, and margin is 0.04. The loss is log(1 + exp(-0.04)) = 0.673347 after rounding, with reward accuracy 1. The changed-input fixture uses beta 0.5, chosen ratio 0.1, and rejected ratio -0.2. Rewards are 0.05 and -0.1, and the margin is 0.15. Beta scales rewards and margin without changing the ratios. Run the command before opening the key. These are expected arithmetic results, not a claim that the command was executed while this artifact was drafted.
The causal-transformer pipeline applies the same objective to summed completion-token log-probabilities. Prompt tokens are masked, so prompt likelihood does not contribute to the DPO pair loss.

sections.title: Train SFT, freeze the reference, then train two DPO policies
paragraphs: The program creates 240 distinct synthetic arithmetic training pairs, 40 disjoint addition holdouts, and 40 disjoint subtraction holdouts. It builds a local character tokenizer from the exercise data, then trains a miniature randomly initialized causal transformer. This is not a pretrained-quality model and its arithmetic quality is weak by design. The default configuration uses a bounded model and records 80 SFT steps, 40 DPO steps per beta, and 320 generated comparisons across the splits. The actual runtime and metrics are UNKNOWN until execution.

Chosen-completion SFT creates the reference. Every reference parameter is then frozen, and independent policy copies train with real PyTorch backpropagation at beta 0.1 and beta 0.5. A prior run record is not supplied with this lesson, so exact completed steps, tie counts, runtime, and metrics are UNKNOWN. It does not establish quality or human agreement. If a run is resumed, record the source identity, checkpoint identity, and compatibility checks before writing new artifacts. Before writing or resuming artifacts, identify the data hashes, tokenizer, model configuration, seed, batch size, learning rate, step targets, beta, and reference hash. Reject mismatches before changing files. Treat those rejection checks as planned until preserved stdout and artifacts establish that they ran.

Each comparison is sent through the rubric in both answer orders. If the answer identity changes with order, score a tie. Report win, tie, and loss counts by beta, temperature, and in-distribution or shifted split. Report swap consistency and decisive winner-versus-loser lengths.

Observed ties or weak arithmetic quality are evidence boundaries, not a reason to fabricate a preferred beta. Preserve generated text, both raw verdicts, seeds, and the empty or completed label fields. A label from the categorical demonstration fixture is not a human label for this transformer run.

paragraphs: The lab should reject overlapping prompts, duplicate training prompts, identical pairs, invalid or nonfinite beta, prompt tokens entering the completion mask, empty completion masks, incorrect identical-pair loss or gradient, nonfinite gradients, reversed scalar gradient direction, reference gradients, and a changed frozen-reference hash. Inspect the checks output and preserve failures. A successful process is not a quality claim.

Interpret artifacts by their field names. Data JSONL files establish splits and preference records. tokenizer.json establishes the local character vocabulary. sft_reference.pt is the frozen chosen-completion SFT reference. Policy checkpoints identify beta-specific models. DPO CSV files contain chosen and rejected log-probabilities, chosen and rejected implicit rewards, margins, reward accuracy, losses, and gradient norms. generations.jsonl contains prompts, seeds, outputs, both judge orders, lengths, and verdicts. evaluation_summary.json contains win/tie/loss, split, temperature, swap-consistency, and length diagnostics. parameter_hashes.json, manifest.json, and run_record.json establish provenance and file integrity. human_labels_pending.csv remains pending until completed.

activity.title: Train a small DPO run and evaluate it against its reference
instructions: Start from an SFT model and record it as the reference. If no SFT model matches your preference data, first fine-tune on the chosen completions (the Preferred-FT approach) and use that as the reference.

Assemble a few hundred preference pairs in prompt/chosen/rejected format. Hold out a set of prompts from the same distribution and a smaller set from a deliberately different distribution for evaluation.
Train DPO at two beta values, logging rewards/chosen, rewards/rejected, rewards/margins, rewards/accuracies, logps/chosen, and logps/rejected for each run.

Generate on the held-out prompts at two sampling temperatures and judge each policy against the reference pairwise, calling the judge in both answer orders and counting inconsistent verdicts as ties. Hand-label a small sample of the same comparisons yourself.
Report win, tie, and loss counts per beta, temperature, and prompt distribution, alongside the training curves.

Begin with the standard-library worked case in `fixtures/worked_case.json`, trace both policy-to-reference log-ratios, scale them by beta, calculate the reward margin and DPO loss, and verify the supplied key with `exercise.py`.
Complete the independent changed-input task in `fixtures/changed_input.json` before opening its key. Use the result to explain what beta changes and what it does not change.

Install `torch==2.5.1` for CPU using the command appropriate to your system on https://pytorch.org/get-started/previous-versions/, then run `dpo_transformer_lab.py` in a fresh output directory through data, checks, SFT, DPO, and evaluation stages.

questions.prompt: Compared with RLHF, what does DPO remove from the preference-tuning pipeline?
choices: The need for preference data
A separately trained reward model and reinforcement-learning optimization with sampling during fine-tuning
The reference model
The KL-divergence constraint in the objective
questions.explanation: DPO reparameterizes the reward so the optimal policy has a closed form, solving the same KL-constrained objective with a classification loss on preference pairs; it still uses a reference model and preference data.

questions.prompt: During DPO training, rewards/accuracies reaches 0.98 and rewards/margins keeps rising, while logps/chosen falls. What is the right conclusion?
choices: The model's generations have clearly improved; ship it
Training has diverged and must be restarted
The model has learned to separate the training pairs, typically by suppressing rejected completions; generation quality still has to be measured on held-out prompts
The reference model is broken
questions.explanation: TRL notes DPO typically widens the margin by suppressing dispreferred completions rather than raising preferred ones; the metrics describe separation of training pairs, not quality on new prompts.

questions.prompt: In TRL's DPOConfig, what does increasing beta do?
choices: Allows the policy to deviate further from the reference model
Keeps the policy closer to the reference model
Increases the learning rate
Switches the loss to IPO
questions.explanation: TRL describes beta (default 0.1) as controlling deviation from the reference model, with a higher beta meaning less deviation.

questions.prompt: Your preference dataset was generated by a model you do not have. What does the DPO paper do in that situation to choose a reference model?
choices: Use the untuned base model unchanged
Initialize the reference by maximizing the likelihood of the preferred completions, to reduce distribution shift
Skip the reference model entirely
Use the largest available model as the reference
questions.explanation: The paper uses the SFT model that generated the data when available; otherwise it fine-tunes on the preferred completions (Preferred-FT) so the reference is closer to the data distribution.

questions.prompt: Your judge prefers answer A when A is shown first and answer B when B is shown first. Under the conservative protocol from the MT-Bench study, how is this comparison scored?
choices: A win for A, because it was evaluated first
A win for B, because it was evaluated last
A tie, because the verdict is inconsistent across swapped orders
It is discarded and the judge prompt is rewritten
questions.explanation: The conservative approach calls the judge in both orders and declares a win only when the same answer wins both times; inconsistent results count as a tie.

questions.prompt: In the DPO paper's human study, GPT-4 given a simple prompt preferred longer, more repetitive summaries than humans did. What does this imply for your own win-rate evaluation?
choices: LLM judges should never be used
Win rates depend on the judge prompt, so the prompt must be fixed, versioned, and checked for verbosity bias against human labels
Longer answers are genuinely better
Only temperature 0.0 samples should be judged
questions.explanation: The authors added a concision-aware prompt and note that GPT-4 win rates are affected by the prompt; the MT-Bench study likewise documents verbosity bias, so the judge setup is part of what a win rate measures.

cues.text: Begin with the pipeline we are replacing. In conventional RLHF, preference examples first train a separate reward model. A second stage then uses reinforcement-learning optimization, typically with sampled responses, to change the policy while penalizing drift from a reference. DPO keeps the same underlying idea of maximizing preference reward subject to a KL constraint, but reparameterizes the reward so the policy can be trained directly from chosen and rejected pairs. There is no separately trained reward model in this DPO formulation and no separate reinforcement-learning optimization stage during this fine-tuning step. For one pair, compare the policy's log-probability to the reference's log-probability for each completion. The chosen-minus-rejected difference becomes the classification signal. The loss is negative log sigmoid of beta times that difference. Beta controls the reference-relative scale. In the TRL documentation, a higher beta means less deviation from the reference, so do not describe beta as a learning rate.

Show a static two-row comparison. Row one lists RLHF: fit a reward model from preferences, then optimize the policy with reinforcement learning under a KL constraint. Row two lists DPO: compare chosen and rejected policy-to-reference log-ratios and minimize the classification loss. Display the formula loss = -log sigmoid(beta * (chosen log-ratio - rejected log-ratio)). Reduced-motion mode shows the same table and formula without animation.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A static two-row table lists the RLHF stages (fit a reward model on preferences; optimize the policy with reinforcement learning under a KL constraint) beside the single DPO stage (minimize a classification loss on the difference between chosen and rejected log-ratios against the reference). Reduced-motion mode shows the table without animation.

Correct the common error that DPO removes preference data or the reference model. It removes the separately trained reward model and the RL optimization stage, while still using preference pairs and a reference-relative objective.

Every DPO reward and margin is relative to a reference policy, so reference selection is part of the experiment design. Ideally, use the supervised fine-tuned model that generated the preference data. That keeps the reference near the distribution from which the chosen and rejected answers were sampled. If that generator is unavailable, the DPO paper describes Preferred-FT: first maximize likelihood on chosen completions, then use that result as the reference. In TRL, leaving ref_model unset uses the policy's initial state as the reference. TRL also documents precomputing reference log-probabilities and a sync_ref_model option for a TR-DPO-style procedure. Treat those as implementation choices to record, not invisible defaults. Each example must contain one prompt and two completions for that prompt. Use one consistent standard or conversational record shape. Finally, inspect what else differs between chosen and rejected answers. If chosen answers are systematically longer, safer in wording, or more formatted, DPO can learn those correlations.

Ask learners to name a dataset they know and list three properties that might differ between chosen and rejected answers besides the intended quality criterion. After responses, distinguish an intended preference, such as factual accuracy, from a shortcut, such as length or formatting. Ask learners to write down the preference-data generator, the proposed reference, and any distribution mismatch before training.

Practice pause: give learners two candidate references. Candidate A is the SFT model that produced the preference pairs. Candidate B is a newer model that was not involved in data generation. Ask which is the default choice and what evidence would justify choosing B. The traceable answer is Candidate A unless a documented experiment supports another choice. If the generator cannot be obtained, the decision record should say that Preferred-FT was used, or say UNKNOWN if that step was not performed.

Now read the training log without turning it into a quality claim. rewards/chosen and rewards/rejected are implicit rewards: beta multiplied by the policy-minus-reference log-ratio for each completion. rewards/margin is chosen reward minus rejected reward. rewards/accuracy is the fraction of pairs for which chosen reward is strictly greater than rejected reward. logps/chosen and logps/rejected are the policy's average log-probabilities for the two sides. Compare all six fields, not just the margin. A rising margin and high training accuracy show separation of the observed pairs. They do not prove that new generations improved. In practice, the margin often rises because rejected log-probabilities are suppressed, while chosen log-probabilities stay flat or fall. That is why a falling logps/chosen is a warning to investigate, not proof of failure. Also remember that implicit reward is reference-relative. A larger number can accompany more policy movement. Holdout generations, shifted prompts, and reference divergence are needed before making a selection.

Allow two minutes for learners to inspect a sample in which rewards/margin rises, rewards/accuracy reaches 0.98, logps/chosen falls, and logps/rejected falls more sharply. Ask them to write: what improved, what did not follow, and what additional artifact is required. Expected feedback: pair separation improved on the logged data; chosen likelihood did not improve; generation quality remains UNKNOWN until held-out evaluation.

Check that learners can explain why the reference-versus-itself baseline has zero implicit rewards and zero margin, and why reward accuracy can be zero under a strict greater-than comparison when both rewards are equal. Ask them to separate a training diagnostic from a quality result. If a learner says a margin increase proves better answers, return to the chosen and rejected log-probability columns.

When no trusted ground-truth reward exists for the real task, use a named baseline and report pairwise outcomes. The baseline is commonly the frozen SFT or reference model. Generate both systems on prompts excluded from training. Keep an in-distribution holdout and a deliberately shifted set, because a preference policy can memorize or exploit training-like cues. Sample at more than one temperature, and record the seeds and the actual outputs. A win rate is not a property of the policy alone. It is a property of the policy, baseline, prompt set, sampling settings, and judge protocol. Fix and version the judge prompt. Report wins, ties, and losses rather than only a percentage. The DPO paper used temperature variation and shifted evaluation as part of its analysis. For this lesson, the required temperatures are 0.5 and 1.2 in the categorical lab, and 0.2 and 0.8 in the supplied transformer lab. Do not silently combine those protocols.

Practice pause: learners draft one evaluation row with baseline name, beta, temperature, split, seed, policy output, reference output, verdict, and judge version. Then ask what would make the row irreproducible. Elicit missing model revision, tokenizer or template, prompt split, sampling seed, and raw judge responses.

The judge is another experimental component. LLM judges can favor the answer shown first, favor longer answers, and sometimes favor their own style or outputs. The MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena study documents these risks, while the DPO paper reports verbosity effects in its own judge study. Use the conservative swap protocol: call the judge with policy first and reference second, then call it again with the order reversed. Map both verdicts back to answer identity. Count a policy win only when policy wins in both orders, a reference loss only when reference wins in both orders, and an inconsistent pair as a tie. Preserve both raw verdicts and calculate swap consistency from them. Separately compare lengths of decisive winners and losers. A longer winning answer can reveal verbosity bias, not better reasoning. Finally, label a small sample yourself or with independent reviewers. Human agreement is not established by an empty file, by fictional fixture labels, or by a judge's confidence. Report the sample size, criterion, labels, and unresolved disagreements.

Check that learners score a swapped-order disagreement as a tie and can name position, verbosity, and self-enhancement bias. Ask them why a high win rate with low swap consistency is weak evidence. Ask what a human calibration sample can and cannot establish. The answer is local calibration of the judge on the reviewed sample, not population-level human agreement.

This offline lab is a finite categorical policy, not a language model. Its response vocabulary is eight fixed strings, and its prompt features are shared across examples. The program first applies chosen-only SFT, freezes that model as the reference, and then performs analytic-gradient DPO at beta 0.1 and 0.5. The supplied code asserts finite-difference agreement, negative-gradient direction, loss reduction, margin improvement, and reference immutability. Those assertions establish mechanics when the program is run. They do not establish transformer ability, open-ended generation quality, accelerator behavior, or performance for any named provider. No numeric snapshots, hashes, sampled strings, or aggregate metrics are supplied here. Preserve the command and complete stdout, and label every unexecuted quantity UNKNOWN. The objective and metric definitions follow the DPO paper and TRL documentation.

The fixture separates training inputs from evaluation information. Eight training pairs use the responses blue, green, safe, unsafe, brief, verbose, calm, and angry. Four in-distribution holdout prompts and three shifted prompts have disjoint prompt strings, while feature lists let the policy transfer learned preferences to new combinations. The policy receives prompt features only. The judge_expected table is available to evaluation, not training, so it cannot act as an answer lookup during optimization. The two human_labels_demo rows are explicitly fictional format examples, not observations. The supplied fixture therefore supports checks for split leakage, shared-feature effects, and judge isolation. Before changing an input, record the original file, edit exactly the requested pair, and preserve both runs. Any resulting metric, hash, or sampled response is UNKNOWN until that copy is executed.

Run lab.py with Python 3.10 or later and no third-party packages. The loader validates response vocabulary, pair fields, nonempty completions, disjoint prompts, feature coverage, and exact evaluation-label coverage. SFT returns a separate model, then DPO copies that model while retaining an unchanged reference. The finite-difference test compares the analytic derivative with a central numerical derivative and checks the optimizer's negative-gradient direction. Negative tests reject duplicate splits, equal pairs, empty completions, nonfinite beta, reference mutation, aliasing, and position-biased judging. The main loop evaluates beta 0.1 and 0.5 on train, in-distribution holdout, and shifted data, with sampling at temperatures 0.5 and 1.2. The code prints snapshots and JSON records during execution. It does not supply their numeric values in advance, so preserve actual stdout rather than inventing results.

Interpret the expected-output section as a contract for a successful run, not as captured output. The program should print PASS markers for the finite-difference and optimizer checks, each negative case, both beta loss checks, both margin checks, and reference freezing, followed by ALL_CHECKS PASS. It also prints snapshots, metrics, and evaluation records. The metrics fields distinguish policy log-probabilities from reference-relative rewards, margins, and strict reward accuracy. Before-training reference-versus-reference rewards and margin are algebraically zero, and strict greater-than makes accuracy zero on equal rewards. Exact hashes, parameter values, sampled strings, counts, swap consistency, and length means are UNKNOWN until execution. If an assertion fails, there is no valid successful-run claim. Archive the fixture, lab.py, interpreter version, command, complete stdout, and any traceback.

Complete the changed-input task only after preserving a successful unchanged run. On a copy, edit the customer reply pair so chosen is angry and rejected is calm, while leaving features, holdouts, judge_expected, seeds, and optimization settings unchanged. Before execution, predict four consequences: the tone-direction update, the edited row's local margin, the shared-feature holdout, and possible disagreement with the unchanged rubric. The edited row shares tone with polite support note, so its probabilities can change without prompt overlap. The team message is another tone training example and creates a conflict that affects final parameters. Do not predict an exact final snapshot or sampled response. Seeded sampling may remain unchanged even when probabilities move. Compare original and modified stdout, SFT and DPO snapshots, tone-holdout metrics, and evaluation records. Mark every unexecuted comparison UNKNOWN.

Use the key to trace decisions, not to replace the experiment. For the edited row, DPO raises the chosen angry contribution and lowers the rejected calm contribution, because gradient descent moves in the opposite direction of the loss derivative. The row's local reference-relative margin should increase for sufficiently small updates, while its pair loss decreases under the supplied assertion. The shared tone feature connects the edit to polite support note; team message also contributes a competing training preference. Therefore the final aggregate tone weights require the actual snapshot. judge_expected remains unchanged and still names calm for polite support note, so a rubric loss after the edit can be the intended consequence of changing training data. The key does not establish exact metrics, hashes, or samples. Those require the modified run's preserved stdout and artifacts.

The full-scale activity is an engineering contract, not an implied promise that this lesson already trains a production model. Clone or download the public learner repository from https://github.com/project42dev/project42-content/tree/main/training/rag-and-fine-tuning-engineering/dpo-and-model-evaluation/lab, then change into training/rag-and-fine-tuning-engineering/dpo-and-model-evaluation/lab before running the commands. The lab contains dpo_transformer_lab.py, requirements.lock, the offline exercise, fixtures, and the pending human-label CSV. The standard-library exercise is designed to run offline. The transformer lab requires an already provisioned compatible environment and uses real gradient training on a miniature random model. Installation, dependency resolution, and training time are environment-dependent and UNKNOWN until measured locally. The core session can cover the theory, arithmetic trace, fixture inspection, and categorical run setup. Reserve an extended lab for environment checks, staged execution, artifact inspection, and human review. A full-scale pretrained adapter remains unimplemented and pending. Do not rewrite code or present an untested TRL command as a validated run. If learners transfer the contract, they must record the exact model identifier and revision, tokenizer and template, data provenance, SFT reference, seed, software, hardware, commands, both betas, temperatures, raw judge orders, ties, and human labels. The evidence is the archived run, not the plan.

Extended-lab planning pause: learners create two schedules. Core session: theory, worked arithmetic, categorical fixtures, negative cases, and evaluation design. Extended lab: environment verification, data and checks, SFT, DPO at both betas, evaluation at both temperatures, artifact review, and independent labels. They must mark installation and training duration UNKNOWN until measured locally.

Before opening the transformer code, make the arithmetic traceable. In the supplied worked case, the chosen policy-to-reference log-ratio is negative 1.2 minus negative 1.4, which equals 0.2. The rejected ratio is negative 2.0 minus negative 1.8, which equals negative 0.2. With beta 0.1, chosen implicit reward is 0.02 and rejected implicit reward is negative 0.02. The margin is 0.02 minus negative 0.02, or 0.04. The loss is negative log sigmoid of 0.04, equivalently log of 1 plus exp of negative 0.04, which rounds to 0.673347. Reward accuracy is 1 because the chosen reward is greater. The independent changed-input case uses chosen ratio 0.1, rejected ratio negative 0.2, and beta 0.5. Rewards become 0.05 and negative 0.1, and the margin becomes 0.15. Beta scales rewards and margin; it does not change the underlying ratios. Learners must run exercise.py and compare to the supplied key. These are arithmetic expectations, not claimed execution results.

Pause for learners to calculate both cases independently. Require them to show the subtraction for each ratio, the beta multiplication, the margin, and the loss expression before checking the key. If a result differs, first inspect signs and beta, then rounding. Do not repair the fixture or key to match an unexamined calculation.

The real transformer exercise uses the same formula, but now log-probabilities come from differentiable sums over completion tokens in a causal model. The program creates 240 distinct synthetic arithmetic training pairs, 40 disjoint in-distribution addition holdouts, and 40 disjoint shifted subtraction holdouts. It builds a local character tokenizer from the exercise data. The model is a miniature randomly initialized causal transformer with two layers and width 64 under the default configuration. It is not pretrained, and its arithmetic quality is expected to be weak. Chosen-completion SFT produces the reference. The reference is then frozen, and independent policy copies train at beta 0.1 and beta 0.5 with actual PyTorch backpropagation. The default run records 80 SFT steps, 40 DPO steps for each beta, and 320 generated comparisons across splits. Runtime, losses, margins, generations, and hashes depend on the executing environment. No preserved run output is supplied with this artifact, so completed steps, tie counts, quality, and human agreement are UNKNOWN. Before resuming, record the source revision, checkpoint identity, and rejection checks. Treat their status as UNKNOWN until the process prints results and the artifacts are inspected.

Have learners read the repository README and write the run identity before launching: exact source revision if available, requirements.lock, PyTorch version reported by the process, data specification, tokenizer, model shape, seed, batch size, learning rate, sequence length, SFT steps, DPO steps, and both betas. Ask what must be rejected before training when resuming. Expected decisions include changed data hashes, seed, tokenizer or model shape, batch size, learning rate, an incompatible target below the saved step, or a DPO checkpoint with the wrong beta or reference hash. These are pre-write integrity decisions. Their execution status is UNKNOWN until preserved stdout and artifacts establish it.

The transformer evaluator generates from each beta policy and the frozen reference at temperatures 0.2 and 0.8 with recorded seeds. Its local rubric checks the last integer against the known synthetic arithmetic answer. That rubric is appropriate only for this closed exercise. It is not a general language judge. Each comparison is evaluated in both answer orders. An inconsistency becomes a tie, and the report groups win, tie, and loss counts by beta, temperature, and addition or subtraction distribution. It also records output lengths for a verbosity diagnostic. The human-label CSV is intentionally empty. Human agreement is UNKNOWN until independent reviewers fill and adjudicate it. Never copy labels from the categorical fixture, and never convert an empty field into a score. Do not select a beta from a headline win rate. Inspect actual generated outputs, shifted results, chosen and rejected metrics, swap consistency, and human review when available.

Pause and have learners classify three facts as observed, expected invariant, or unknown: a reference hash should remain unchanged, the exact win count before execution is unknown, and an empty human-label field is pending rather than a negative label. Ask them to mark the source artifact that would establish each fact.

Audit the artifacts rather than trusting a final status line. Data JSONL files establish the splits. tokenizer.json establishes the local vocabulary. sft_reference.pt is the chosen-completion SFT reference. The two policy files identify beta-specific results. CSV files hold actual SFT and DPO losses, chosen and rejected log-probabilities, implicit rewards, margins, accuracies, and gradient norms. Generations JSONL preserves prompts, seeds, outputs, both raw judge orders, lengths, and verdicts. The evaluation summary reports distributions, temperatures, swap consistency, and pending human review. Parameter hashes and a manifest make changes visible. Negative checks should cover duplicate or overlapping prompts, identical pairs, invalid beta, completion-mask errors, nonfinite gradients, gradient direction, and reference freezing. If a reference gradient appears or its hash changes, stop. For transfer, the custom model cannot load external checkpoints directly. Provider-neutral candidates include Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, NVIDIA, Z.ai, and Kimi, plus commercial model families only as evaluation candidates. Check architecture, tokenizer, chat template, license, context rules, hosting, and adapter compatibility for the selected provider. No compatibility or quality is validated here.

Ask learners to map each claim to an artifact: frozen reference to parameter_hashes.json, human status to human_labels_pending.csv and evaluation_summary.json, and actual metrics to the CSV files rather than prose. Then ask them to explain the adapter contract: completion-only log-probabilities, seeded generation, frozen reference, the DPO formula, preserved metrics, swapped-order records, and model-specific tokenizer and checkpoint tests. A named provider is a candidate, not evidence of compatibility.

Guide the mechanics lab in two phases. First, learners run the standard-library categorical policy from the supplied repository files and preserve the exact fixtures, command, and stdout. They compare beta 0.1 and beta 0.5 on train, in-distribution holdout, and shifted prompts, reading chosen and rejected log-probabilities separately. They inspect temperatures 0.5 and 1.2, both judge orders, derived ties, and length diagnostics. They then hand-label a sample without looking at the rubric first. Second, learners use the supplied changed-input task: alter only the specified preference, predict the gradient and shared-feature effect, run the copy, and compare snapshots and holdout results. The tiny lab is a real finite categorical policy with analytic gradients, not a spreadsheet, but it does not demonstrate transformer language ability. Do not present fictional human_labels_demo entries as observations.

Begin the knowledge check after learners can explain the sigmoid loss, the role of beta, the reference choice, and the six required training fields. They should also be able to distinguish a rising training margin from improved held-out generations, compute a swap-consistent win or tie, and identify why human labels remain pending. Accept UNKNOWN when the learner correctly identifies an unexecuted or unlabelled quantity and states what artifact would establish it.

If that generator is unavailable, the DPO paper describes Preferred-FT: first maximize likelihood on chosen completions, then use that result as the reference. Treat those as implementation choices to record, not invisible defaults. Each example must contain one prompt and two completions for that prompt.
